utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness. There are two administrative matters before cross-examination. The first, it would greatly assist us if we could know how much cross-examination there may be of the witness in order to make arrangements for calling or not calling the next witness, who would be travelling some distance to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we have in mind three hours, but then the amicus may have some questions. I don't know who's representing the amicus today. Well, we'll give some time for Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It looks as though the whole day may be consumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would have thought effectively the whole day is going to be taken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And 30 seconds, with your leave, in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I've explained I have no further questions of this witness. I understand there are some observations that she wishes to add to the evidence she gave yesterday, and I'll sit down while she makes those observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, if you want to add something to your evidence, now is your opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to say that everything that I wrote down in my book entitled "The Serbian Army," published in five editions, and everything that I made a note of, I did publicly in the cabinet of the minister of the army, pursuant to permission from General Simovic. I should also like to say that he authorised it all twice; the first time was for the Nin publishers and the second time was for the book itself. And I would like to say that what you have before you, all the documents you have before you and the book, that that is thanks, first of all, to General Simovic, and also thanks to President Milosevic, of course, who could have prohibited it all and put a ban on it had he wanted to. I continued to maintain that I did my best to make a note of all the facts and it was just supposed to be a report to my people and I never imagined that this would be evidence in a court of law. I should also like to state that in agreement with the Prosecutors, we agreed, in fact, that I should be a witness here and that I should say everything not only as a witness for the Prosecution but everything else that I know about what was happening during that period of time. So I am ready and willing to answer any questions to the best of my knowledge and as far as I am able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Glisic, in the examination-in-chief -- I don't think my microphone was switched on, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Gajic-Glisic, in the examination-in-chief you skimmed through some matters briefly, so I should like to ask you now to give us some more detailed explanations about some of these issues, to make them clearer, and in order to make certain distinctions which I just saw some intimations of in your explanations, probably due to the shortness of time you were not able to go into them in any depth. But before I do so, before I go on to my questions, I should like to ask you something with respect to your status. I'm sure you know that until yesterday morning, until you entered this courtroom, you were treated as a protected witness by -- and you had a pseudonym and we were also told that we would be having a closed -- a private session. Did you ask for that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come that you suddenly changed your mind and decided to testify in open session?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My sons asked that of me. They said, "This is an opportunity, an occasion to take -- to state that you're not a spy, to take all this onus away from you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you make the decision, yesterday or earlier?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday morning I asked the gentleman, Mr. Nice, whether I could ask Their Honours before I begin, Your Honours, can I now speak quite openly and frankly? Because that's what my sons have asked me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I asked you that question because when you had the protection -- protective witness regime, I was given some very limited information about this because nobody is supposed to know who the witness is except my two associates. And then, of course, it is very difficult to collect the necessary information and material I need. But Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you've clarified that issue, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise to you, but my life is an open book. In my 17 books, I have described my life, and I shall be happy to tell you anything you need to know about my life publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clear up some matters first, some things that I think have remained fairly -- have not been described sufficiently because of your -- the briefness of the time you had. First of all, the question of volunteers. May we observe -- or rather, is it true and correct that there is a drastic difference between volunteers, the ones you dealt with in the sense of assistance or recording and keeping records of them and the paramilitary formations which you just mentioned by the by yesterday. You mentioned certain formations such as the Dusan Silni, the White Eagles, Paroski, Mauzer, et cetera, and you said yesterday that they weren't within the system and that you had nothing to do with them nor did the ministry have anything to do with them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there the difference is quite clear; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what you say about volunteers applies exclusively, therefore, to the volunteers who signed up to the JNA or the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA in 1991 was a regular army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia throughout its territory; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, depending on where it was under the command of the Territorial Defence of the municipality in which it was a Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commanders of those staffs, commands, were the presidents of the local community or municipality, and all together they were under the command of the JNA, and I don't think I'm wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, with respect to these other units which you mentioned, you also mentioned, for instance, the Serb Volunteer Guards of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also mentioned Captain Dragan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that Serbian Volunteer Guard of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was under the command of the Territorial Defence of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was also linked up with the MUP of Serbia, and the MUP of Serbia from time to time would mobilise certain members for assistance to the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, so I'd like to ask you to explain it to me. Because as far as I understand it, you received that information from Simovic. On what grounds were you able to conclude that the Serbian Volunteer Guards was linked up to the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that information, first of all -- or rather, we received that information from Minister Zoran Sokolovic. Now, if you will give me a little time, I would like to give you an example to illustrate how I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, please, but just briefly, because I have to take care of my time.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information that I was to find a mobilised recruit quickly for personal reasons, and I was told that his wife was in a very difficult situation, that she was actually dying, and that he had been mobilised and I was asked to find him and have him return to Belgrade. As a wife and mother and woman, I did my very best to find the unit he had been mobilised into, but we failed to find him in any of the war units of the army. And then General Simovic asked, "Well, Zoran, where can we find Pelovic? Who mobilised him in the first place?" and I said, "You General; we did, General." And he said, "How come you?" "Well," they said, "we sent him to help Arkan." And I rang up Arkan's headquarters and Mr. Pelovic told me, "Well, my mother gave birth nine times and I came here to fight. You don't suppose that I'm going to desert and leave home [as interpreted] just because my wife is going to give birth." And then Mr. Zoran Sokolovic said, "Well, we mobilise occasionally members from the reserve force of our police to provide assistance to Arkan's volunteers." So it is the present-day president of the Party of Serbian Unity, in fact, that's the man I'm talking about, and that was the information I had and I apologise to the Prosecutors for the fact that I have some personal, very deep emotional ties with the daughter of Professor Dr. Citic [phoen] from the medical military academy. She was married to Mr. Pelovic, in fact, and Dr. Citic at that time operated on my son. And I did my utmost to have this man returned from the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Pelovic was in contact -- actually, he was in the Party of Serbian Unity, that is not at issue.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Serbian Unity was, Mr. President, formed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite true. But I don't know that he recruited on the part of the ministry. All he did was -- I think he independently, as a patriot and an intellectual, became involved in some assistance over there.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but he was president of the King Alliance of boxers, I think. I don't know the sports organisations. But as such he was on the war list of the police, the Serb police, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I assume that it was voluntarily that he joined the Serb Volunteer Guards. It wasn't the police that could send him to the Serbian Volunteer Guards because the Serb Volunteer Guards was never a formation of the police force.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Sokolovic at the time claimed it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that you might have misunderstood Sokolovic, because that is impossible. But I assume that you are speaking in good faith and to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am speaking in good faith, and I would like whole-heartedly, first of all, to help you and my people, but primarily by telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. So that's the only way that can be done. Tell me this now, please: All the things you did with the volunteers, that the Ministry of Defence did vis-a-vis the volunteers, was it in conformity with the laws, the rules?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Nice even asked you whether I knew about some provision or decree that is brought in by the government or the ministry.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Provisions are enacted by the government at the proposal of the various ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as Captain Dragan is concerned, he was here and said that he came from Australia alone. Nobody called him or invited him to come. And he wasn't within the composition of the Ministry of the Interior at all.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said differently to us at meetings, and if you would like, I should be happy to show you the original -- my original notes, in fact, that I typed out and brought to your cabinet. And Their Honours can ascertain and establish that those notes date back to those times. So I don't know the other side of the coin; all I know is what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume you know that Captain Dragan exclusively became involved as an instructor on different occasions and so probably in that capacity with respect to the training of individuals from the police. But that has nothing to do with his participation as a volunteer somewhere on the battlefront, outside Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that he was sent or invited by Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic, and that was all directed by Jovica Stanisic, and that with him there were another six in that first departure for Knin, there were six more specials from the state security who were in Knin as instructors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He testified here in this courtroom and said that he had come alone himself and that he worked exclusively and as an instructor, that he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was not in any combat, did not take part in any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not my recollection of the captain's evidence. I seem to recollect that he was involved in a combat operation involving a police station. We can check it out. But in any event, I mean, the important thing here is what he may or may not have said to this witness. That's what's relevant. What he said here is not relevant necessarily to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Stanisic orchestrated that, his arrival. And you know that in 1991 Stanisic was not head of state security.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Stanisic at the time was the chef de cabinet of Mr. Zoran Sokolovic, and the head of state security was Mr. Janjackovic. I had very good cooperation with Mr. Zoran Janjackovic, and with Mr. Stanisic I just had several conversations with him over the phone with our special telephone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as my information tells me, he wasn't even Sokolovic's chef de cabinet. But never mind, we're not going to pursue the point.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you would like to see them, these are notes from Botic's villa, from the meeting held there. I wrote that because my conscience dictated that I take these notes without any intentions or any thought of having an opportunity at some point in the future to show them. So these are my notes from that period, from the meeting with Captain Dragan, and he speaks about his combat activities there in that area over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he is providing you, actually, with information about what was going on and where he was involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that he was involved in combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he is providing you with information. So this is a sort of debriefing of Captain Dragan by the service and by you too from the ministry, to get to know what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see the meeting -- or rather, the meeting was organised by the police and state security, and he was brought to Botic's villa by a police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But let's clear this up. They were gathering information, intelligence, about what was going on over there. He was over there, so then he provided you with the information you wanted to know from the defence and the police, to tell you what was going on over there. So this link, this connection actually boiled down to providing you with information about -- and intelligence about what was going on over there. Had you sent him there, I assume you would have known what was going on over there and you wouldn't have expected him to have to tell you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he began talking of his own bat. The meeting began that we were engaging him to train volunteers in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's a different matter altogether, whether you're going to engage him for training volunteers, but the meeting that you were having and the notes you made from the meeting meant collecting information from him as a man who was present in the area at the time, and that's what he talked about here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Now, something else, please: Please, as we are talking about volunteers, we have now drawn a clear distinction between those volunteers that you kept records of and the paramilitary formations that had nothing to do with the state. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you now to briefly go through a few documents that I have here and to tell me whether they confirm that, as far as volunteers are concerned, all this was in compliance with the regulations. For example, I have here instructions on the receipt of volunteers into the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please just help me by telling me the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have not received this from those who called you to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. This may be a document which the accused has got and you won't have. So, Mr. Milosevic, if you hand it over so the witness can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look. Here it talks about the way in which volunteers are accepted, about their health checkups, their security checks. All these aspects are familiar to you, I assume, but please take a look at this instruction and tell me whether it's authentic or not. This is an instruction on the receipt of volunteers in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the method of admission of volunteers to the Territorial Defence under tab 12(A), and I think that here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry, we must -- we must try and follow this in a fairly orderly way; otherwise, we shall get in a muddle. Could you just look at that document which Mr. Milosevic has given you. Could you confirm, if you can - or if not, say so - that it is what he described, that it's authentic. He says it's an instruction on the receipt of volunteers in the Territorial Defence. Can you confirm that that is right, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps before -- just while you've got it, could you help us with this so we can identify the document. Who gave the instruction? Who was it to? And what is the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the -- pursuant to Article 9 and so on of the law on defence, Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, number 45/91, the minister of defence and the command of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia have issued an instruction on the admission of volunteers to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we -- is there a date on it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not on the document itself, no. At least, I don't see one. But I think that I have the law on defence from that period, and -- this is the same instruction here from the law that was published during the period while I was the chef de cabinet, and it's a valid document, Comrade President, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I'm giving you this instruction, so everyone can see that there is no mystification here. An instruction was given as to how people were admitted, what conditions they had to fulfil, that they had to go through training, that they had to be fit, that they couldn't be under 18 or over 60, that according to the regulations - and I marked this - they had to undergo a security check.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this instruction was issued only a little later, a little bit after volunteers began to arrive, because this was adopted in July. The instruction was signed by General Tomislav Simovic, who was officially appointed minister of defence on the 26th of September, at the Serbian parliament. And these documents that you have given me are practically a page from this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this identical?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, there's no issue. This -- these instructions are in accordance with the law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the law under which we operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. So this is not contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous Translation Continues] ... Do you want that document exhibited, although it's documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will hand you the whole law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But we have got -- just for a moment. We've got an awful lot of paper in this case, so we're trying to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. keep it down to a minimum. But thank you for volunteering that. If you'd like just to keep it for a moment. And then if something turns on it, we'll, of course, come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have a torn bit of facts here, but we will put it together. We will admit it. We'll let the Prosecution have a look at it. We'll give it the next D number. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the registrar go first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 203, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document number 19, which I have already given to the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will have better versions probably of this document, complete versions. We'll make them available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And when the complete version is available, it can be substituted for what the accused has handed in. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the complete version. But because it was faxed, it's a little torn into three bits. But nothing is missing. It contains everything from the preamble to the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is correct, Comrade President. All the paragraphs start with the same words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they're in the same order.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was one thing I wanted to clarify with you, but please let us go more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous Translation Continues] ... have you now got a complete version?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Got it. And in English. But, of course, not copied at the moment in enough numbers for everyone, because we don't know what documents are going to come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If that can be put -- that can be put together with the original exhibit. We'll rely on the registry to clear it up. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, if possible let us try to save time. So please could you please go through some other documents I have here now. There is also an instruction here on the admission of volunteers to the JNA of the 13th of September, 1991. And this instruction was signed by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, which also contains all these aspects of their admission in accordance with the law and also emphasises - and I have underlined this here; it's paragraph 5 - it underlines there must be a security check when admitting volunteers according to the rules of the security service, and these must be strictly adhered to. And the same provision exists in the instruction we have just seen. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For this reason, I find it impossible to believe, and I would say it's just a rumour that people were released from prison to be sent to certain units.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply said what Minister Zoran Sokolovic told us in the cabinet of the minister of defence. I am familiar with the decree you mention. Unfortunately, I don't have a copy here, because we were not part of the JNA. The Ministry of Defence of Serbia was separate from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And you had no competence over the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at this instruction, please. You're probably familiar with it. Because I wish to tender it into evidence. This is a complete document, and the fax has not messed it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While the witness is looking at it, Mr. Nice, I have a recollection of seeing this document. I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour's recollection is, as ever, spot on. I think it's Exhibit 406, tab 14, if information coming to me is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll let the witness comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have seen a similar document in the Office of the Prosecutor, and the way in which the stamp has been placed on it and the words "military secret, confidential," and the seal at the bottom, all this, except that the signature is illegible, indicates that -- it's in compliance with the way things were done at the time. So I'm 99 per cent sure that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to another document, which is in fact a photocopy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- let us just make sure that we get this right and in order. That has been exhibited. We will make a note of that, but I would be grateful if the Prosecution would check the number and perhaps make sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll check. I haven't yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, who's been able to advise me and is usually master of the documents, suggests 406, tab 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit this one. It may be a slightly different version of the same. But we can note -- it will be on the transcript -- that it's the same number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, while we sort this out. We'll get a new D number for this one. Is it the same? Very well. Further inquiries show that it's the same, so we don't need a new number. Yes, we'll look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the instructions were issued pursuant to a decree issued by the government of the Republic of Serbia? Mr. Nice was mentioning a decree law, but there is no such thing. There is simply a decree on the conscription of volunteers. And in Article 1, it says that this -- that it prescribes the way in which volunteers may join, and then it goes on to talk about replenishing the JNA with volunteers in accordance with the federal regulations. So this is fully in compliance, and it was issued on the 14th of August, 1991. This is a photocopy of the Official Gazette, which is authentic. It's an authentic Official Gazette in which laws are promulgated and all legal and physical entities interested in legislation receive this. Would you take a look at it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again, I think that's a document we've had, the 14th of August, 1991, Republic of Serbia. Again, my recollection is that we've had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll search for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a document -- or rather, the document I was talking about. I apologise for calling it a decree law. I am an electro -- technical engineer, so in my vocabulary this is what we called in the cabinet, this is what we called it. We were doing something that was in accordance with the law. So yesterday, and when preparing to testify here, I always said that everything that I did and everything that we did there we did pursuant to documents and regulations, and as I was told, with President Milosevic's knowledge. We didn't do anything behind Comrade Milosevic's back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everybody did their job, I hope, Ms. Gajic-Glisic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so too. I worked sincerely. I worked from my heart for the defence of the poor Serbian people on the war-affected territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, there is one other thing I would like us to clarify: You know that the state organs responded on several occasions to the existence of several paramilitary formations and they endeavoured to -- to get everything done in accordance with the law and to eliminate these formations. You yourself said -- we won't list them again -- that these units were not part of the system, that they had nothing to do with the state, and as you say later in your statement, it was organised by various parties and so on.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I described this in detail in my book, and I would like to draw attention to the period -- or rather, to the chapters in which Pejicic talks about the way volunteers were organised by the Serbian Renewal Movement, and they were sent there bypassing the legal regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Serbian Renewal Movement was the largest opposition party of the time.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the decree issued by the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last exhibit, Your Honour, I think is 406, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 13. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Whiting for tracking that one down, and I'll hand the original, or the accused's version, back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not my version. It's the official text from the Official Gazette, which was officially applied. The Official Gazette publishes exclusively regulations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have that. We have it, Mr. Milosevic. We'll just see if it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same, and so we don't need a new number for that. And you can have the -- your fax back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I draw your attention to the order on recruiting volunteers during an imminent threat of war of December 1991. And this mentions all these criteria that we've talked about. And I will read you only paragraph 7 and 8. I hope you are familiar with this as well. What's this? Oh, this is it in English, instruction. Very well. I'm glad I also have it in English. It's good to accumulate as much paper as possible. So paragraph 7, the volunteer units that are now engaged outside the units of the JNA. So there was a constant problem of various units that were outside control. You remember this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is an effort on the part of the Presidency to put everything under control, everything -- and it was very difficult to do this in that chaos, and it says that these units and volunteers that are now performing certain military tasks or are within the units of the JNA have to regulate their position in the armed forces and bring it into compliance with the provisions of this order. And on the territory for which the units of the JNA are responsible, they are to remove all individuals and volunteer units that fail to join the JNA in the manner prescribed by this order, that is, those who are not subordinate to the chain of command and to discipline, so they are not to be used in any other way. And the next provision relates to the volunteers who fail to comply. There were certain volunteers who reported but then again did not respect discipline. And in paragraph 8, it says that "... persons found in uniforms and with the insignia of members of the Armed Forces of the SFRY but who have not joined the Armed Forces in the prescribed manner and regulated their position in compliance with this order will be subject to legal measures." So the highest organ, the collective Supreme Commander, which is the Presidency of the SFRY, ordered that order be introduced and that those who were not members of the armed forces and who were there on their own initiative be removed, and they say that the unit -- the commands of the units are duty-bound to remove all such people from their area of responsibility. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not connected to the JNA. I am aware of this, but I have not seen this order, this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's an order. Would you have a look at it to see if it's authentic or not, because I wish to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just can't see the signature, Mr. Branko Kostic here, who at that time was the president of the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can't see that but you can see his name?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can see his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the Official Gazette, it isn't signatures that are printed but just the name of the person that has signed it, along with the date, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you on that score. But I don't know how far this is under my competence, how far I can approve this or not approve it, in view of the fact that the date is the 12th of December and the government fell on the 12th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you're not competent to approve that. I accept that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I should like to insist, Mr. May that, this order be tendered into evidence, because it does indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can be of assistance, Your Honours. I do believe that this is a true and exact document. But I should like to emphasise once again that it doesn't come under my competency, giving a judgement on orders of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will -- we will give it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 204, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, that when you wrote your book, you wrote it to the best of your understanding and knowledge of the events that were taking place and your participation in them.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that what you wrote then you stand by now and you think the same.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I should like to remind you of several excepts from your book. And I can see you have the book beside you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you turn to page 51, please. And General Simovic is responding there. He is answering some questions. They asked him, "What are the goals of the policies of Serbia, whether to reject the Croatian policy and to have Yugoslavia remain as a whole or to create a Greater Serbia, as some people are claiming?" Have you found that passage?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Am I quoting from your text exactly?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now we come to Simovic's answer. Simovic says the following: "Serbia at times of crisis, as well as during the KPJ, Communist Party of Yugoslavia, comes out in favour of each and every nation having the right to declare itself and the right of national minorities to be citizens on a footing of equality in Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has the Chamber found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. In English --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 35 at the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should just like to ask us to follow this passage. Is that it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the crisis blew up and the military aspects, Serbia opted for a peaceful settlement to the situation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the armed forces -- armed force began to be used in Slovenia and then in Croatia. The Serbian government considered that the Ustasha paramilitary formations carried out massacres as a result of that which are unfortunately repeating themselves in history once again. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, you go on to speak about the Second World War, et cetera, and then you continue: "In all this, the Yugoslav People's Army, pursuant to a decision by the Yugoslav state presidency, is given the task of setting up a buffer zone between the Ustasha formations of Croatia and settlements inhabited by Serbs from times gone by. It is not a question of creating a Greater Serbia but it is a question of protecting the Serb population which through force of circumstance is the most numerous in Yugoslavia and, therefore, populates the greatest territory." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was that an exact description given by General Simovic in response to the questions asked?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have here the authorised first version and this second version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to prove that to me. I'm just quoting from your book. And you stand by what you say there. And you consider it to be true and correct. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, turn to page 54, please. And it is in the middle of that page, in the middle of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the Court is looking for the page, it may be assisted by noticing that at the beginning of the tab 9 there is an index that approximates B/C/S to the English. This should be, if it's 54, it should be something in the order of page 37, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am quoting once again and asking you for your confirmation whether that was so. And I'm quoting you. Simovic says, "From the very beginning of the secession, the Serbs were said to be guilty for the war for the sole purpose of asking that Serbs be treated as equal citizens with the citizens of Croatia." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say, "I think that the Serbs in Yugoslavia -- that Serbia and Yugoslavia is one and the same," and Simovic's response is this, "So I'm asking you now why don't you stand up to this?" And he said, "I'm sorry that you didn't notice that the JNA is making efforts to protect the Serbs from genocide and not to cause an armed struggle but to work towards creating conditions for a political settlement to the crisis, which means peacefully, by peaceful means." Is that right, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic? Is that what it says in your book?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this an exact description of the situation which prevailed at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was waged by Serbia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then I should just like to ask you a few more things. We have Minister Simovic's reactions. It is on page 76. And the heading there is "The Reactions of the Defence Minister Lieutenant General Tomislav Simovic to the Serbian Renewal Movement." And he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's page 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- that as the Serbian Revival Movement, which was very strong in creating the situation, Simovic says, "The prevention of the slaughter of the Serbian inhabitants in Serb lands and freeing our sons, members of the JNA, who were made -- held as prisoners in the barracks. Isn't that clear to everybody by now?" Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I will confirm that thousands and thousands of soldiers, children from the age of 18, were shut up in the barracks in Croatia, that they had no electricity, they had no water, they had no food. And the women in black would send out their love to them and sing for them around them but that they were in a very poor situation, these children there. And I also wish to say - and it is very difficult for me to remain calm in saying so - that for days and nights I did my best to -- through our connections and links, set up links with Croatia, and that I asked them to tell us what was going on with those children there, the soldiers there, those children of 18, 18 years old, are they still alive, how are they? I wanted to get any kind of information that I could, but connection would always break down and all we could hear was the term "nazocni" being used, the duty officer. Now, that is the worst period in my life and I can't rid myself of those images to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe you there when you say that. Now, would you please take a look at page 144, the penultimate paragraph. This is Simovic's explanation once again, and he says this: "Different armies clashed. The one wanted to liberate Osijek; the others wanted to take over Western Slavonia although that was not the object." Is that what Simovic says, this was never a goal, this takeover? And he continues and says, "Because we were fighting for places where the Serb population was in the majority but each one pursued his policy and tasks. And when they would encounter a trap, they said that the army was disloyal and would not help them in the fighting."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these people who were outside anybody's control called the army a traitor army; whereas, the army tried to play, as Simovic had said - and I quote him from your book - the role of a buffer zone between the attacks and attackers and to protect the settlements which were supposed to be protected and defended from these individual, mutual clashes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Comrade President, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in the next sentence he goes on to say, "The army did not wage a war of conquest. They were fighting for places in which the Serbs lived as the majority population and the fighters from those parts wanted to liberate their own thresholds." He goes on to explain that. "But not in places where they were in the minority and the fighters from those places wanted to defend their own thresholds." And that's where the confusion sets in that he talks about, and which the State endeavoured at the time to calm down and not to allow this chaos to break out, the chaos that was developing and the situation to which Simovic reacted. Isn't that so, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting thinks page 105. You're probably there ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in -- in page 104, in the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I've got to withdraw for just a couple of minutes. Mr. Whiting will remain, representing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And take a look at page 169 now, please, the end of that penultimate paragraph. Otherwise, the chapter is headed "Secret Bad Sides and Open Good Sides." "The army has no pretension with respect to any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslav republic, but it cannot sit with its hands crossed while some of its garrisons were still found under siege," said Simovic. Was that so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The barracks were under siege and Croatian wives were standing around. A large number of barracks throughout the territory of Croatia had been held under siege. The soldiers were left without electricity, food, without anything, in fact, and that is why we organised the column of buses taking mothers to visit their sons. The title of that chapter was, "Secret Faults, Open Virtues."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should like to draw attention to page 152, the middle passage. Simovic says, "There were 14 truces thus far and all of them broken by Croatia. During those truces, according to the data which I have, your country" - because he's being asked by a Hungarian journalist, it seems - "Hungary is flying planes into our air space and weapons are being imported through your country." Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I should like to remind you, Comrade President, that there were municipalities with a majority Hungarian population and that the danger existed of new conflicts breaking out all the time, because the Hungarians wanted to join up with Hungary, the state of Hungary. And I think that it was in agreement with you that the foreign minister of the day, Vladislav Jovanovic sent a letter of protest to the embassy of Hungary, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was quite a lot of that going on. And probably it is as you say it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. We need to find this latest quotation. Can the Prosecution assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet. I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 222 of the book. It is the middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 222? You said 122. Let's find -- let's find 222 then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 232.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, page 232.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We will find it. Just one moment while we find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "So far there have been 14 truces or cease-fires." It is how the middle paragraph begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the middle of the page, 167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you've found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, "14 truces, each violated by Croatia," and then goes on to speak about the infiltration of weapons, et cetera. And then one more sentence - that comes at the end, the epilogue - on page 313, you say, "The minister of defence, without an army, the president of the republic, without the capacity of having the Supreme Command." I'm just quoting that for the moment. Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, you know that it was always our option to favour Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that in the constitution of Serbia, which was written in such a way, that Serbia has all -- enjoys all the competencies when the crisis was in its throes, when the constitution was written, in fact. But in one article of the constitution it says that the competencies and authority enjoyed by the federal state, pertaining to the federal constitution, are executed in the federal state and in conformity with the federal constitution. Therefore, is it quite clear that the Republic of Serbia, with respect to the Yugoslav People's Army, did not have any competencies?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You were not the Supreme Commander of the Yugoslav People's Army. And as far as I - if Their Honours will believe me when I say this - as far as I was able to note, the army -- or rather, the person who had the weapons wielded the power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is quite usual and customary, especially in war situations. But according to what you said, and because Mr. Nice did not let you finish what you were saying, you said that there are laws which show that the apparent authority was in the hands of the president of the republic, as if I had taken over this competence from Simovic's hands. Neither Simovic nor myself had any competence and authority over the Yugoslav People's Army, nor could we have had it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. But let me just remind you that when I was speaking about national defence and the law on national defence and the competencies and authorities there over the Defence Ministry, having said that General Simovic did not have any authority, not even to measure up with an accountant, as I put it, I said that pursuant to an article of the law, that is to say, Article 6 of the law, which stipulates that the president of the republic in the organisation and preparation for defence heads the armed forces in peace and war, including authority to solve organisational and personnel matters in the Territorial Defence. So I wasn't speaking about competence and authority in respect of the JNA. That doesn't come under my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember that since you were in the Ministry of Defence yourself that it was even the command of the republican staff of the Territorial Defence that was nominated and appointed by the SFRY and not the president of the republic in any of the republics until these other republics had seceded, but in Serbia, for instance, that was at that time the competence and authority of the Yugoslav state presidency? I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. But allow me to say that I can't know everything, and I don't claim that I do know everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. You needn't know everything. That's quite true. So you talked about an event here. You said that when there was some sort of crisis where in those conflicts in Slavonia, as far as I can remember, a large number of civilians was at risk and members of the Territorial Defence, and you said this was in October or November 1991, and I asked Simovic to entreat the people in the JNA to fly over in planes, not to drop bombs, but to fly over in order to help them.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that you issued the order. I didn't say that he was able to issue an order to them. I said that both you and he entreated them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I am asking Simovic, because he was a general and before that he was the commander of a military district, the Skorpion military district, and he was a very high-ranking general, I was asking him to use his influence and to entreat them to fly over in order to help those people there.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What's in dispute here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I said something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Nothing was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous Translation Continues] ... just remember, Mr. Milosevic, this isn't a private conversation. It's got to be interpreted. So will you leave a pause, and would the witness be kind enough to leave a pause after he's spoken. Thank you. So remember the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, this event that you described is something I wanted to clarify again for a simple reason, because you as an eyewitness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are saying that I asked Simovic to ask his colleagues from the JNA to fly over for the simple reason, as I said, is that the claim is being made here that I commanded the JNA. And you as an eyewitness say that I had to entreat Simovic to entreat those people of his over whom he did not have any command either to fly over. Had I been commander, I would not have had to ask Simovic to ask them to do that; I could have ordered it. Is this clear or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's go on. You described -- I made a note here during your examination-in-chief -- you described a meeting between Simovic and Hadzic where Hadzic was to be introduced to the Serbian public because he was representing the Serbs from Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem at the conference in The Hague. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've confounded two time periods. But let me hear your question to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted you to explain what you said later without being asked, in connection with this, that I didn't even know who Hadzic was. I wrote down, "Milosevic asked Simovic, Who is Goran Hadzic?" You said that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was already in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was already on his way to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was already in The Hague as a representative of the citizens of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I am not contesting the right of the citizens in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to elect Goran Hadzic and send him there as their representative. This is not in dispute and this is not what I'm asking. But is it in dispute that when he was already in The Hague as an elected representative I didn't even know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Comrade President, when Goran Hadzic came to the Ministry of Defence, Goran Hadzic didn't even know what he was president of. Later on you asked, "Well, who in fact is this Goran Hadzic?" General Simovic called General Nenezic to ask where Goran Hadzic was coming from. General Nenezic said that Goran Hadzic was a relative of his, that he had been a warehouse-keeper in the area, that General Nenezic wanted to push him as a politician and that he was in fact the self-styled president of the area and that it was too late now to correct all this because Goran Hadzic was already in The Hague. I describe that in detail in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have time to go through that. I just wanted to establish on the basis of your testimony as an eyewitness of these material facts that at the time that he was already at The Hague and I asked Simovic, Who is Goran Hadzic? I didn't even know who Goran Hadzic was.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume you didn't have all the correct information, that General Nenezic and the others around you had misinformed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't even remember General Nenezic. What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was organising the rebellion of the Serbs over there in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was General Nenezic already retired?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he and General Pekic were the ones who went to those areas. Often they went back to their youth and raised revolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But these were pensioners, old-age pensioners who were doing things on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you mentioned something about a conversation of mine with Simovic - I just want us to clarify this - in connection with the Territorial Defence in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. You said that there was some confusion and that Hadzic appointed Stojicic as the commander of the Territorial Defence. Did you say that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Stojicic was a volunteer, that he went there as a patriot to help?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he went there as a volunteer. Nobody told me that, that he had gone there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Goran Hadzic appointed him commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the source of the confusion, because he was a policeman from Belgrade who went with his special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't go with a special unit, he went in another way, but he went there as a volunteer and patriot. And Goran Hadzic appointed him commander of the Territorial Defence. Is this in dispute?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it's not in dispute either that I said to Simovic, "There's some confusion over there. Hadzic appointed Stojicic commander of the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell me, please, before we move on, I understood that you wanted to say more but due to shortage of time Mr. Nice interrupted you, so I will use my time now to ask you what did you know about the sufferings of the Serbs in Croatia while you were in the ministry and before and after your work in the ministry? What did you find out about the sufferings of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was dreadful. It was dreadful. The Serbs were expelled from their homes. Serbs had to flee with only a plastic bag in their hands. Those rooms in the 13th of May that were used for training and to put up those who were being trained, the first Serbs who were expelled after the arrival of Franjo Tudjman in power, the first refugees were Serbs. These Serbs would come and they had nothing, nothing. Many of them lost their families. They didn't know where their families were. We received photographs of slaughtered Serbs. I think, Comrade President, that we prepared a bundle of those photographs for you as evidence for The Hague, but unfortunately I gave the photographs I had to my friends with approval of a colonel from the -- who approved that this be given for them to show their families in Switzerland. They were all burnt. I apologise to Their Honours, what I have to say when I remember those pictures, their limbs had been cut off and pushed into their mouths. There were very many refugees. For example, at that time in Serbia there were 150.000 refugees from Western Slavonia. And according to the lists and our knowledge, in Western Slavonia there were 60.000 people, 60.000 Serbs, and suddenly in Serbia 150.000 refugees turned up and most of them were in Novi Sad, in Sid. Representatives of trade unions came to see us because they were unable to find firewood, heating fuel, there were no classrooms, there was not enough money to buy books for those children. They didn't have food. At the time it was awful. On the other side, we had Milan Babic, who kept coming to the cabinet and kept threatening to bring 300.000 Serbs more unless we mobilised Serbs from Serbia to go and defend the Serbs from Croatia. It was a terrible time. At that time, children were imprisoned in barracks in Croatia, mothers -- mothers wept, screamed. They burst into the government buildings. Nobody dared go and face them. I think you asked Simovic to send me to talk to those mothers, and I wept in front of them, and I begged them to go on our knees, to bring our sons back and to look for them, even if we were killed. There were -- it was terrible. In Serbia there was not enough fuel. There was not enough food. There was not enough firewood. The situation was terrible. Those who were mobilised came back from the war front. We had invalids who arrived without legs, without arms, and we were unable to provide them with their basic means. They would sit there with their crutches in front of the government building, and we had to jump over them. The situation was terrible. Sometimes I didn't leave the cabinet for days, and we worked for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. days on end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You could probably say a lot about the sufferings of the Serbs in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- at the time, but due to time constraints, I can't ask you to do that. You provided here an interview given by Lieutenant General Tomislav Simovic on the 19th of November, 1991. I took this from your tab. The ERN number is 02905739. When I say "yours," I don't mean -- I'm not talking about you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have the original text here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think -- I think, Mr. Milosevic, before we go into the document, it is in fact time to adjourn. So we'll -- we'll return to it. We'll get the tab number from the Prosecution. I take it to be one of their documents that's being referred to. We'll adjourn now, and we'll come back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, that you are aware of the fact that the General Staff of the JNA, in that period, that is, the period when you were working in the Ministry of Defence, when talks had already started with Mr. Cyrus Vance, the emissary of the UN, about the arrival of the UN forces -- so do you know that the General Staff kept insisting that the barracks be unblocked so that the army could withdraw from there without casualties and without conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember applying to Lord Carrington that there were agreements between the JNA and Croatia, that this should be made possible, but that this was not made possible?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I now draw your attention to this interview. And I have told you the ERN number. I will not read it all, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's tab -- it's tab 1 of Exhibit 568.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the middle column of the interview, the question is put whether the JNA was mostly a Serbian army according to its composition, as was often heard. And his reply was, "It is just partly correct. According to its ethnic structure, the JNA has still got approximately 27 per cent members of other nations and nationalities, aside from the Serbs and Montenegrins. It means that realistically its permanent and variable peacetime structure mainly consists of members of the most numerous nation, the Serb one in this case, which was the case before as well but to a smaller extent. The fact that that ratio is now somewhat bigger is a consequence of the past political and military developments in the territories of Slovenia and Croatia and the behaviour of leaderships of certain nations and nationalities in Yugoslavia. I can say that the JNA was turned into a Serb army, referring to its structure, exactly by those leaderships who invited their peoples to abandon it and start fighting against it." Is this an indisputable fact and is what General Simovic says in accordance with the actual situation and the events in the period that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Simovic gave this interview to Mr. Ivica Dacic in my presence, in our cabinet. And it's an authorised interview. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the first column, he speaks of the protection of the Serb people from the renewal of genocide. You have just spoken of the sufferings of the Serbs in Croatia, of the 150.000 refugees then in Serbia. Is it contested that the Serbs at that time had very serious reasons to be afraid, because they were exposed to physical extinction?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of his first reply, in the first paragraph, he says, "Objectively the Yugoslav People's Army did not have any other option facing the situation when the Ustasha units were adamant in their intentions to destroy the Serb populace." Was this the reality everyone was facing?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all very afraid of this. At any moment Serbia was threatened with attack, and you know that it was attacked in Sid. Sid was attacked. You were in The Hague at the time, and we were all communicating at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was shelled from Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the territory of Serbia. You go on to say -- just let me find it here -- that there was a meeting between General Jovic, who was already retired, is this correct, at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was at one time in the peacekeeping forces of the UN?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One of the peacekeeping missions that Yugoslavia took part in.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he knew Marek Goulding who was the assistant of the secretary-general for peace operations.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he met him in private?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this conversation that you describe in fact took place because everyone was interested as it was at the height of Cyrus Vance's activity and negotiations all over Yugoslavia with representatives of the authorities of the Krajinas, with us in the Presidency of the SFRY, in the Presidency of Croatia, and so on, about bringing in peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Marek Goulding was the first person to propose bringing in peace forces, and you accepted that the moment it was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because this was in the context of negotiations held by Cyrus Vance. Marek Goulding came along with him, and he was the assistant for peacekeeping operations. You drew up this note, which is tab number 7. I won't quote it in its entirety, but it boils down to, as I see, a telephone conversation between Jovic and President Milosevic from your cabinet, the cabinet of the minister of defence, where he is giving information to you and by telephone to me about his conversation with Marek Goulding.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you drew up these minutes in order to have information recorded on what was essential in that conversation; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an effort to take down everything to the best of my ability. And immediately afterwards I typed out these minutes and brought them to your cabinet personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now I wish to draw your attention to page 2 of these minutes. In the paragraph before last, he's describing how Goulding came to Yugoslavia to see about the possibility of bringing UN peacekeeping forces to Yugoslavia. And he says that they talked about the Yugoslavia of 1918 to 1941 through 1945, and he understood the role of Germany in all this, accepted the thesis about the Fourth Reich and the revision of the Second World War. "He knows what Milosevic has done for Serbia. I familiarised him with what Gorbachev did. I told him the US will be sorry for breaking up Russia," and so on. And then you say -- not you, but you drew up the minutes -- he asked who Babic and Hadzic were and whether they could provide guarantees. Everybody then wanted guarantees that nobody would attack the UN peacekeeping forces. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That they would accept the peacekeeping forces of the UN. That was our stance from the very beginning, to accept the UN peacekeeping forces, to put an end to all conflict, and to seek for a peaceful resolution of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was your sentence, which I was not allowed to take down. I could only take down what was said inside our cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was asking about the volunteers and so on. He said he knew who the black-shirts were and asked for a guarantee from Paraga. You know who Paraga is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leader of the paramilitary organisations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, did these paramilitary forces commit atrocities against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
