utterances.text: Yes, as far as we were able to ascertain. And General Vracarevic spoke of this, and this is in a part of my book entitled "The Dogs of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And at the end of this paragraph, he says, "The principle of the UN boils down to understanding the technicalities of separating the sides at contact point." And he was confused about the behaviour of the Croats and the request that peacekeeping forces be deployed along the administrative borders. He's not clear about the volunteers. Then we come to the demand that a Serbian army be established. And as this idea was not accepted by Serbian policy, the advocates of a Serbian army were recorded as volunteers, registered as volunteers. And then there is mention of the "Guard" and that a company does not go over 1.000, and so on. Is it in dispute that he says that "The creation of a Serb army was not well received in Serbian political circles"? We were in favour of Yugoslavia, Yugoslav institutions and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at that time we simultaneously worked on the draft bill on the armed forces of Serbia. You know this. But the idea, after it was published in the press on the 5th November, was ferociously attacked by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We did not want to make the position of the JNA more difficult, or of any Yugoslav institution in any way. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. And in my book, I speak of the reorganisation of the JNA in the existing borders, the new borders, whether it would be a rump Yugoslavia or a Yugoslavia consisting only of Serbia and Montenegro, or whether it would be just Serbia alone. And this draft bill on the armed forces of Serbia had three versions, three variants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you remember that in April the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was promulgated and that according to the constitution the army of Yugoslavia was established?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992. This was several months later, after those others were recognised, when the FRY was established and the same joint session of the parliaments of Serbia and Montenegro on the part of the Yugoslav parliament that stayed behind, a declaration was issued that the FRY did not have territorial pretensions towards any Yugoslav state. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was after I was driven out of my job in the ministry. So this does not belong to what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your testimony. Yes, I accept that, and I will not ask you about this further. In your book, as I see in the summary, you mention me quite a lot. In your book, I came across a passage where you -- and please correct me if I'm wrong, because I had to skim through the book -- but you mention me in five places. For example, on page 60, the chapter is entitled "Genocide Before the World." And you say the following in that first sentence there: "During those days, there was a meeting, a tete-a-tete, between Simovic and Milosevic." And then he started to say -- this is at the bottom of the page -- what had to be done urgently, and then goes on to explain what the urgent tasks were. He says that all photographs and tapes, which we have and which relate to relations with respect to the genocide of the populace in Serbian Krajina, should give to the -- be given to the Ministry of Information for a book to be published and for documents to be compiled for The Hague. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this talks about efforts to hold political talks and to present the truth as clearly as possible about the actual state of affairs in which the Serb population in Croatia found itself and the dangers which were ultimately the reason for which the UN peacekeepers arrived and proclaimed zones under their protection, UN-protected areas. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when The Hague is mentioned here, it is mentioned in the context of the peace conference and not in the context of this institution.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was on the 18th of October, The Hague Conference. Put me right if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991. I don't know the exact date, but it's not important. The important thing is that that first meeting that you describe here in your book has no -- nothing to do with any armed operations, but what it is about is the gathering of information geared towards political negotiations through the mediation of the international community. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And as far as I remember, you were in The Hague on the 18th of October and later on, on the 5th of November, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were several occasions.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise, a lot of time has gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of meetings, but the point of what this is about is that the talks related to the preparation of information with a view to political negotiations and talks and not any kind of military operations.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does it say "military operations" here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it doesn't. I just wanted to clear that point up.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Yes, that is correct. And I believe I described it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 112, where you mention me once again. And you say the following - and this is in the paragraph that is in the middle of the page - "Our position at this meeting, and it is the Assembly meeting, expressly demands the formation of a Serb army. It was clearly requested that the president of the republic, Slobodan Milosevic, take on the role of the Supreme Command of the army of Serbia. And that is something that was not supposed to be uttered then and I don't suppose today either." Now, this explanation, that we were quite clear in our stance in favour of Yugoslavia and for preserving Yugoslavia and that we considered it indispensable to support the Yugoslav People's Army as a Yugoslav institution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. But I don't contest the fact either that at the same time we were working on the law for armament of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's another matter. Professional work to prepare a bill.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice referred to a secret law or bill of some kind. There was no secret bill or law. You worked to prepare the law as every ministry does within the field of its responsibility, and once it is prepared it goes to the assembly boards and goes to regular assembly procedure. It is never secret.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't understand Mr. Nice to say that it was a secret law. What I understood him to say, that everything that was done in the ministry was to a certain degree of secrecy and confidentiality. And what was being done there couldn't be presented to the public just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. And that is natural for ministries such as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Defence Ministry, the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Comrade President. And this was a precedent, in fact, that somebody should put forward and state what was going on in a series of articles in the Nin magazine, and that led to a whole affair that was equated to the Watergate affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there were no consequences?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The issue of secrecy was, I think, initially raised in a neutral way and I think it was the witness's first answer that spoke of the way in which matters were dealt with and I will have to check the transcript to find whether she used the term "secret" or not. I'm not sure that I used the word "secret" after that. But the evidence emerged from the witness's mouth, not from mine on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record, the passage of page 79 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the third place in your book, where you mention Milosevic again, in the context this time of your description of what Simovic talked about to Babic, that is page 159. Have you found page 159?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then Babic replies - and that's how the page begins - and in paragraph 1 he says, "The President is accusing us -" the President, meaning me -- "is accusing --"

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's 139. I apologise for reading it out wrong. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Babic's answer was -- and you recorded this, because you attended the meeting between Babic and Simovic. He says, "The President is accusing us, and first of all I was surprised because I asked you to leave the TO as an armed force and not to withdraw the JNA." And Simovic says, "This has nothing to do with the withdrawal of the JNA, nor was that what was being asked." And then you go on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that Simovic was already quite irate and said what Babic was asked to do was neither a request made by Milosevic or Simovic. And he adds, "What am I here? Just a balance between the two of us? I want you to know that that is so because that is the sole condition for the arrival -- the only precondition for the deployment of the United Nations forces. Babic would not accept it," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The record should show, as Judge Kwon said earlier but it wasn't taken down, that this appears at page 100. It's important that we have for the record not only the B/C/S version but also the English version so those who come after us can follow what's being said. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, he is emphasising, and I repeat the last sentence of that quote, the one that I selected where my name is mentioned: Simovic says, "I would like you to know that that is -- I want you to realise that this is so because that was the only precondition for the deployment of the UN forces." So this is prevailing upon Babic to accept the arrival of the UN forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember, you had a great deal of problems with Babic at that time, who did everything off his own bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this third excerpt from your book, where you mention me, that too is geared towards a political settlement and the arrival here in actual fact of the UN forces for which we are advocating, which Serbia is advocating and which the president of the SFRY advocated and which I was in favour of personally.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all in favour of the arrival of the UN forces. We all advocated that. And we were even prepared to make all the concessions necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Then you go on to mention me for a fourth time in your book, once again. It says, "Put off until eternity." This is page 202 of your book, I don't know what the page is in English, where you say that "the proposal came from this ministry," which means your ministry was proposing that General Veljko Kadijevic - General Veljko Kadijevic at that time was the Federal Secretary for National Defence, the number-one man in the JNA - and the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, should have a meeting and decide what to do next. "Simovic insisted that this should come about as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then on the next page, it goes on to say that "Since the problems that exist --" or rather, "The JNA has great problems because of all these events." And we've already mentioned that. And you go on to say in paragraph 2 on page 203 that "The clear question should be asked which the key problems are in taking over the territorial organs and territory, how far we have come in that regard, and what it is that the Republic of Serbia has still not done in order to make the mobilisation successful." So we are talking about that part of the competency, that was the sole competency that the Defence Ministry had, that is to say, with respect to mobilisation, keeping military records, and so on and so forth. It was that portion which belonged to the republican ministry, that came under the republican ministry, with respect to administrative matters having to do with military recruits from its territory.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just remind you that the Defence Ministry of Serbia did not have any competence and authority over the mobilisation of military conscripts unless the reconnaissance and notification service -- unless you mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for adding that. So it only had these very limited duties.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is why it is stated here that it should be clearly seen what Serbia has failed to do, because the question keeps cropping up about why the problems with respect to mobilisation, what we hadn't done and which was under our competency.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mobilisation process had been taken over by the military departments, which had now come under the Yugoslav People's Army and its departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, on page 204 -- it is the last sentence of this chapter, on page 204, it says, "The Milosevic-Simovic-Kadejivic meeting never came about. Nor did a Serb army ever come about."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was the last conversation that you and General Tomislav Simovic ever had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have enumerated four such talks, four such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph of page 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You enumerated four such conversations. And you also mention me on one more page, 212. You say, "They can't decide about that." And then you go on to say, "A meeting has been scheduled for tomorrow with President Milosevic, which is compulsory, and General Panic with his associates, Jokic and Sokolovic, Jokic, Commander of the Territorial Defence, Minister Simovic, to be present. Minister Simovic should come a little earlier. However, this meeting was called off at Milosevic's request as there would be no meeting and a solution would follow." I mention this because no meeting ever took place. So judging by what you write here in your book, I had three Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. meetings in actual fact with Simovic, the one where I mentioned -- and one of the ones I quoted was a meeting with Babic, where he says that they were not the demands made by either Milosevic or Simovic but it was a precondition for bringing in the UN forces. So -- and now this fifth instance where I mention the meeting wasn't ever held; it was called off. Is that right, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comrade President, how many meetings you actually had with General Simovic I did not count them all. There was another meeting where I arrived with General Simovic, and then I wasn't able to enter your office. So that was one more meeting. And General Simovic told me that he was going to have a meeting with you, he was going to you for a meeting. When I wrote this book, I did not write it for the Tribunal. I did not write it for check ups of this kind. So I can't say exactly how many meetings you did have in actual fact. All I can do is to speak about the telephone conversations which I attended, the ones you had. And so I speak here about what you call - I don't know - firsthand, secondhand, or third-hand knowledge. I just told you what General Simovic told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. The reference in the last passage is 154 in the English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, I'm not questioning your goodwill to testify to the best of your knowledge and to answer questions frankly and sincerely. All I'm doing is and I assume you will allow for the possibility of the fact that you couldn't have known certain things, when you're talking about Marek Goulding, for example, as making the proposals and that it was Cyrus Vance's idea and that it is indeed called the Vance Plan. But that doesn't matter. I'm just quoting that by way of an example. But you allow for the possibility that perhaps you didn't know everything fully, perhaps you didn't hear properly about certain things in a situation of tension. You might have even interpreted things differently.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, but all of us are prone to make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's take another example here, something that I would say is fairly - how shall I put this - radical. Take a look, please, at your statement in which you say the following: "That it was precisely because of that law, the one that was being drafted, that General Zivota Panic --" What was General Zivota Panic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the 1st Army District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, commander of the 1st Army

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think he was the commander for combat in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He stormed into my cabinet wearing full military gear, combat gear. And I'll read paragraph 103 of your statement, which states as follows: "General Zivota Panic entered Milosevic's cabinet with his escorts. He allegedly accused Milosevic of creating a Serb army. General Panic forced Milosevic to order the Prime Minister of the Serbian government, Dragutin Zelenovic to tender his resignation so that the government of Serbia could not adopt a law on the armed forces of Serbia." Don't you think this to be highly improbable?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comrade President, the secretary, Mrs. Mira, called me up on the phone and said, "Dobrila, don't give out any information to the information media because General Panic, in full army combat with all his entourage, stormed into Mr. Milosevic's office and solutions will follow, settlements with follow." So that was the conversation between myself and your secretary. I didn't even take this too seriously -- or rather, I didn't understand the seriousness of the situation. A little before that, in our cabinet, we had the presence of Mr. Dragutin Zelenovic. He was there talking to Simovic. And we leafed through the documents that had already been typed out, the documents compiled in Batajnica on the 13th of May. The president of the commission was Buda Kosutic. We were discussing having this discussed at a closed government meeting. So I attended that particular conversation when General Simovic went to attend a government meeting. He came back some 20 minutes later and said, "The government has fallen and Zelenovic has tendered his resignation." And then I told him what Mira, your secretary, had told me prior to that. And he said, "Well, a putsch has taken place." I said, "What putsch?" He said, "A coup d'etat."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, from what you're saying, General Simovic informed you all of his conversations with everybody else. I can see that that would emerge from the way you put things. Now, I'm not entering into his methods of work. However, as far as I'm concerned, I never informed my secretary about the contents of my conversations with anybody. Nor did I have this kind of relationship with her that I felt it necessary to inform her of my conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. The witness can't answer for that. She can't know what you told your secretary. All she can say is what the secretary told her, and that's her account. Now, if you have some information that that account is wrong, of course you can put it. But you can't -- she can't answer for your relations with your secretary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness, in point 103, says that General Panic forced me. I don't know how he could force me. But she says he entered armed to the teeth. That is a complete untruth. Panic never entered with an entourage of any kind into my office. He did come to see me, but he wasn't armed to the teeth, of course, and not to threaten me and to frighten me and to make it impossible for me or for Serbia to pass a law of any kind. So I hope you will allow for the possibility of the fact that you, Witness, understood this wrongly, because my secretary could never say something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am here under oath, and I remember very well to the present day the sound of her words, and I stand by what I said, that that is what Mira told me on that occasion. Now, what happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, I really don't want to enter into what secretaries talk about amongst themselves, but can you conceive of a situation in which any general could storm into my office, whether Panic or anybody else, armed to the teeth and force me to do anything and that I would be frightened by that and to say, "All right, that was a joke. We're not going to pass a law and Zelenovic can tender his resignation"?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact that on the next day Zelenovic resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course you didn't attend the cabinet session at which he resigned.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Zelenovic gave as the reasons for his resignation? It had nothing do with the enactment of the law on the armed forces. It had not even been prepared for the parliament.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't give any explanation, apart from the letter I handed and which you have amongst these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Zelenovic's letter?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does the letter say? Tell me, please - since you handed it in, I don't have it with me now - but what does Zelenovic say in that letter? Every Prime Minister has the right to resign.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very brief, just two sentences. Should I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please read Zelenovic's letter of resignation.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you help me? Can you give me the document number? What's the tab? Since --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot. I have too much paper here. I can't help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. We'll -- we'll see if the Prosecution can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're identifying it from rather a large number of documents, but we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why don't you go on to some other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. topic and they can look and we can return to it. It's a matter for you. If you want to wait, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Of course I don't want to wait, because time is precious, Mr. May, but this claim is so unbelievable for anyone who knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not a matter of comment. This is the first time I've heard that someone committed a coup d'etat in Serbia and the government fell for this reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was General Simovic's explanation, and I wrote it down for my book and not for the Tribunal. I stand by the conversation we had in the cabinet. That's how I noted it down. And it's not for me to think about what really happened in your cabinet and what you talked about with General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Panic, madam, General Panic had no competence. He was the commander of one strategic -- he had no competence to deal with any political issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, that's not for the witness to answer. That's what she says she was told happened. Now, we will have to decide in -- in due course what weight to put on the -- the evidence. I suggest we find some other topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just found the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The letter has been found. Perhaps you could read it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Read it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Dear Comrade President, In accordance with Article 93 of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and Article 45 of the rules of proceeding of the parliament of Serbia, I hereby resign as the Prime Minister of Serbia. I take this opportunity, Comrade President, to thank the deputies for their understanding for the work of the government and for keeping their integrity and my integrity and for their cooperation with this office. I wish you all much success in your further work. Yours sincerely, Dragutin Zelenovic." It's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this is resignation of the Prime Minister. What has it got to do with the law on the army and what has it got to do with military matters at all?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before writing this letter, he was sitting in the cabinet and talking to General Simovic about the draft bill on the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could have sat in anyone's cabinet and talked about various bills that were being prepared, but he did not resign because of a particular bill. The Prime Minister would resign in connection with a bill when it was rejected by the parliament, not when the cabinet hadn't even considered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all a matter of comment. You've heard what the witness -- what the witness has said. Now, do you want that letter exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have heard what the witness said. Yes, you can exhibit it or not, but these are incredible things, really. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's available in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll get the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she read it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt. Let us have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Defence Exhibit 205. For the record, Defence Exhibit 204 is also exhibited as Prosecution Exhibit 387, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, you say that Simovic was then replaced. You keep using the expression "the replacement of Simovic."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, are you aware that when the Prime Minister resigns, then the president of the republic gives a mandate to somebody else to form a cabinet? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, the resignation of the Prime Minister means that somebody else is given the mandate of forming a cabinet and this other person then proposes the composition of the cabinet to the parliament. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but previously consulting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether they consult me or not. Well, there are some matters they consult me on and others they don't, depending on their importance. But what I'm asking you is this is not about the replacement of Simovic. It's simply that the term of office of the then-Prime Minister had been terminated and the new person who had been given the mandate to form a government selected his own ministers, and this is nothing unusual, because everyone who forms a government does so according to their own views and their own plans. So the Prime Minister resigned and the new Prime Minister is forming his cabinet. That's quite normal, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this would be true, Mr. President, had not terrible repression followed on this. Marko Negovanovic, a general, came and said, "You wanted a Serbian army. I'll give you a Serbian army." And then he said, "You, you brought all kind of riffraff here. You brought Mosa [phoen] to my cabinet. What Serbian army? What law? Nothing will come of this."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was doing his job and he was dealing with the law on the army, which was part of his competence. Other ministers who arrived did their work. But you were not the only ministry there. There were 20 ministries in the government.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all ministers were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the new Prime Minister kept some and changed others. What's so strange about that? A new cabinet was established. He took some ministers from the previous government because he felt he had to keep them. What's so strange about this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite, Mr. President, but after that I was punished, and then I was banished from the ministry, and then I was banished to Batajnica, and then General Kuzmanovic and General Negovanovic allegedly ordered that I be liquidated urgently, and then Colonel Slobodan Jovanovic took me out barefoot, to run out on the 13th of May to save my life, and then even you intervened, according to what Mr. Milo Kligojevic [phoen] told me, and he said my life was not to be imperilled, and then General Aca Vasiljevic, who worked on part of the draft law on the armed forces of Serbia was taken to prison, and many other things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did Serbia have to do with Vasiljevic? Vasiljevic was then in the General Staff. It has nothing to do with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He attended meetings every Sunday -- or rather, every week, and he consulted General Simovic about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't go into that, but here is another absurdity for you. I don't want to suggest by my means that you have told a lie. No, I simply want to draw your attention to the fact that you must allow that things may not have been the way you thought they were, especially as it was quite impossible for certain things to happen in the way you say, for Panic to burst into my office with weapons, for all of this to have something to do with the law on defence, and we were advocating Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've already -- you've already covered all that. We've been over it. Let's go on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, then, be so kind as to look at this, which is also absurd. Just let me find it. From what I see here - I'll read this out to you, although in paragraph 111 there are many things - but I'll start Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with what it says near the end of paragraph 111: "On the 14th of February, 1992, Tomislav Simovic arrived unannounced, which was unusual. He usually called before coming and announced his visit. This time he was devastated. He showed me the decision on his retirement. He told me that he had been called back from annual leave to the General Staff of the JNA and that there was no one in his office when he arrived. In the meantime, he had been promoted to colonel general and he worked in the General Staff of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of December, he was promoted to the rank of colonel general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he was moved to the General Staff, transferred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was no longer a minister but he was a general and he was given an assignment.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please pay attention to this part of your statement. You say - I've just read this - "There was no one in his office when he arrived." I don't know why there should be someone in his office when he arrived. Probably as colonel general he had an office of his own, he didn't share it with anyone. And it says, "After some time, General Tumanov arrived." Tumanov was in the security service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think that at the time he was a colonel and not a general.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this, he was promoted to general very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this doesn't matter really. I heard that he worked in the security service and that he did a good job.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General Tumanov arrived after a time and put a request to -- a retirement request on the desk.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He put this request on Simovic's desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Simovic was supposed to sign it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this request was already drawn up, and Simovic just had to sign it and he would be pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he put this request on his desk, pointed a pistol at his right temple, and ordered him to sign. He put the request on his desk, ordered him to sign it, and put a pistol to his temple. General Tumanov ordered him to sign this; otherwise, it would look like suicide. Did you write this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write this. General Simovic stated this when he came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He stated this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me about this. And that night he told Zoran Bogavac about this and many other things, and Zoran Bogavac promised never to make this public. General Simovic immediately afterwards, faced with enormous threats and pressures, changed his story and said, "Oh, yes, I wanted to retire. I didn't get where I wanted. I didn't manage to set up a Serbian army. The Serbian variant has fallen through, I want to retire." And very soon he changed the story that he told me when he came to see me, and this same story he told Zoran Bogavac in his house that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, I don't want to put you into a difficult situation, I really don't, and I don't know any of the -- the character of the dramatic relationships between General Simovic. But I have here a photocopy of the request by General Simovic. I have a photocopy here. And it has been registered in the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. The number is -- and it is authorised, the authenticity has been certified, et cetera. So here you have the request for General Simovic's pensioning off, that you say Tumanov put a gun to his temple, but this entire request was written out in hand, written by General Simovic himself in his own hand, so he couldn't have placed this on the table with a pistol to his head. And it says "Request for cessation of AVC," which is active military service. And then the title, sent to the chief of the General Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY in person. All this has been written out in his own handwriting, and it says, "In view of the fact that I have over 40 years of service, I hereby request that the AVS --" that is to say the active military service -- "that my active military service cease forthwith." And the next sentence is, "Please forward my request to the PSU" or, rather, the personnel department. The 15th of January, 1991 is the date. Colonel General Tomislav Simovic, followed by his signature. So this completely refutes what you claim, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, and it is very improbable. This is the first time that I've heard anything like this, that somebody placed a pistol to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we've -- we've heard enough now. You're supposed to be asking a question. I've allowed you to read the letter. But you must now show it to the witness and allow her to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's tab 10 of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This seems to me to be General Simovic's handwriting. This is General Simovic's signature. General Simovic could not have had 40 years of service at that point in time. As far as I recall, General Simovic was born in 1933, and we're talking about 1991 here. So it says here that this document was registered on the 15th of January. I'm talking about the 14th of January. According to my notes, it was the 14th of January. I have nothing to say in this regard, pursuant to this document. I stand by what I said previously and what I wrote previously, that that was how it was and that the general told me that story on that day. And General Simovic, under different pressure, would very often change his statements. I should just like to ask you to take a look at page -- a page in my book. It is page 293, where it -- "We're all posthumous." And even when he authorised my manuscript in its first version prevented me and prohibited me from having it printed. And then he changed his mind and authorised the portion he had banned, banned being printed, and allowed me to publish it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one matter that I want clarified. The year was given as 19 -- January 1991. Is that the right year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The month of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it is. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that on the document, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But it was translated or came out as 1991. That is why I was questioning it. Yes. Do you want this exhibited?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. May. This is a notorious fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Hand it -- hand it in, and we'll give it the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 206, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it, Mr. May, that yesterday Mr. Nice had said that General Simovic would be testifying. He mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I said no such thing at any stage. And while I'm on my feet, by the way, just to correct something else. The references to "secret" were both made by the witness in answer to neutral questions by me, the one about a level of publicity and the other to like effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been given a copy of Dragutin Zelenovic's resignation. I don't want to read it out again, because I'm quite sure that the witness read it out very correctly. I simply wish to draw your attention to the fact that this resignation was addressed, as it says, "Comrade President." That is not me. I don't want that to be misunderstood, because you have different expressions for that. But this resignation was addressed to the person it was intended to, the President of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, because the National Assembly nominates the government, appoints the government. And that's what it says in this translation here. So I just wanted to draw your attention to that. And he did this pursuant to the rules and regulations for this kind of thing. The president of the republic proposes the mandate. The National Assembly appoints the government pursuant to proposals of the mandate. And it is only the Assembly that can dismiss or appoint anybody. And the oath is taken before the Assembly. I don't know. But I understood it that an announcement was made yesterday to the effect that General Simovic would come in to testify. But if I have understood incorrectly, then I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anybody mentioning that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Comrade President, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's make it plain. There was no such announcement yesterday by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just note that Mr. Nice said yesterday while he mentioned about the book, "We are -- we will be hearing in due course Mr. Simovic." Yes. It's on page 27793, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That simply must be a transcript error. I have never had that in any mind and I certainly have no recollection of saying that. I'll look it up and see what it must be a mistranslation or a misrecording of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I remember I heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also remember that well, having heard something to that effect. That's why I brought it up. And I wouldn't have any reason for bringing it up except for having heard it with my own ears. And as you can see, His Honour heard that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, the transcript as we know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- let us have the matter clarified. But the answer is no. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, is it contested or not that you in your statement in many places, or to be more specific -- well, yes, in many places don't only write about things you heard directly and saw directly but you're talking about things you heard from others as well and also the conclusions you made about what you heard and which was grounds for the observations you make?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used my diaries, my own notebook, my book, my knowledge in order to write out my statement in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But without a doubt, in many places you write about what you had heard from others, mostly from General Simovic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you sure that it was from your observations and from the things you heard that the right conclusions always emerged, that you made the right conclusions about what you say and specifically, in concrete terms, the matters I asked you about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I not been sure, I would not have put them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me this now, please: I noticed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's being dealt with -- I'm so sorry. Forgive my interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich has found the passage that His Honour Judge Kwon has referred to, and I can pretty well recollect what was said and -- certainly what I intended to say and indeed what I think I did say. I think you'll find this is an early passage of the examination-in-chief, and I was putting a question of one of those passages which didn't require evidence in full from the witness. And I was saying that this was checked for the content of its accuracy by a man called Simovic, of whom we will be hearing in due course. Certainly what was intended to be said -- because at that stage you -- well, you may have known, but from the evidence we got to that far, you wouldn't have known exactly who we were talking about. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you in your CV mention many things that do not have a direct bearing on your testimony or the time during which I performed some political function. But could you please clear this point up. You say that upon return from America, you wrote a report, 360 pages, but that work of yours was banned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, that was in 1983. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean banned, when it wasn't published in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this manuscript of mine was taken away from me by the state security.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the manuscript -- as the manuscript probably is still in existence in the archives of the state security somewhere, and since I believe that you might dig it up, and so that I should prevent you from saying that I was telling lies or not telling the truth, in agreement with the OTP I put that sentence in, to the effect that all of us in our lives have some things that happened to us and which should be mentioned for me to be completely pure and clean here. Of course, that has nothing to do with you. I didn't know that you existed at all at that time. But of course, some information and knowledge that I got there, heard about, wrote down. I was young. I didn't believe in some of those things. I was told that I wasn't to speak about those things or write about them, nor could I publish them anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Regardless of the fact that this was all happening in 1983 - and I really don't know anyway, nor can I have any idea about it all and what you say - but what was the name of the member of the state security who advised you not to publish that work of yours? What was it that you wrote in that work that was so dramatic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously you know about it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is obvious or not. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that on your face clearly, and quite obviously you know all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, regardless of what you assume, can you tell us what it was that you wrote at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I listened -- and this seemed to me to be a joke by Kundara [phoen] or Orwell's 1984 to the effect that communism would topple in the whole Eastern Bloc according to the domino system. It would fall down like dominos and that the Soviet Union would disintegrate and that the Serbs would be disbursed and resettled and up rooted from its territories. And that in Yugoslavia there would be blood up to the knees and that Kosovo would be joined up with Albania, part of Macedonia, and Greece and that a greater Albania would be formed, and so the siptars could breed over there and that part of Macedonia would be attached and conjoined to Bulgaria and that part of Vojvodina would be joined to Hungary, that there would be great divisions in Europe generally, and that that was a long-term plan that was being prepared. Now, at that time, my country was the greatest and most beautiful country in the world, and I found this all to be a science fiction, highly improbable. And I wrote all this down from one day to the next, and I wrote a diary, in manuscript form, 360 pages long, and I thought I'd publish it and that this would then be a big book. However, when I handed it over to the director of the Obecija Novina [phoen] publishing house, they called me to come to their premises. They introduced me to a man whose name was Liki --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go further into all this. All I wanted to hear from you was what you wrote. And that what you wrote seems to be coming true, what you heard over there when you were in America.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Comrade President, I told all this to General Simovic in our first conversation and I told him that all this was -- had been realised, right according to the domino system and in the periods of time that they told me about over there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that there? Who told you about this plan? Who put it forward to you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very young then. I was a correspondent for the paper Komunist. I was a journalist but also an engineer in the Sloboda [phoen] company and dealt with innovatory work there. I was an enthusiast, very enthusiastic about the work I was doing, and I published my first book "Mother, Give Birth to me Again." It was published by the Obecija Novina publishing house in Gornji Milanovac. A businessman turned up from America and he spoke Serbian very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting but my time is very short. I just wanted to hear about this all. I'm sure the history of it all is very interesting, but we don't have time. But who did you learn about these facts from, that is to say, how the Serbs would be disbursed and how Yugoslavia would be destroyed and how a Greater Albania was to be created and all the other things that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From people very close to the then-President Reagan. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1983, was it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in my country, they ordered me not to speak about that to anybody. They forbid me to speak about it to anybody, to publish a single word of that, that I had to keep quiet about it and that it was something that wasn't to be spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really don't want to enter into all that, because to the present day I couldn't understand the reasons for which you were not allowed to write all that down or, rather, to publish it, because everything else about Yugoslavia was published. I don't remember that there were any bans of any kind. But -- so this is -- these are things you learnt from people close to the American President, President Reagan, in 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Pope, in 1982, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we are now getting a long way from the subject. You've asked the witness about something which you've been allowed to do. It may have affected or not the credibility. But it sounds as though we're getting a long way from the topic. Anyway, it's time to adjourn. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I only ask you to tell me how much time I have left, as I have many questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got 22 minutes -- 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Mr. May, the statement of Mrs. Gajic-Glisic has 307 paragraphs, 307. And there's the book, plus the binder. If I were looking only at the paragraphs, it would mean 100 paragraphs an hour. That would add up to three hours. So I have to ask for more time. I cannot go through everything, but at least allow me to go through part of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, how long do you think you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I always took account of the time and try to make the best use of it. I think that 15 or 20 minutes would be sufficient for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have additional time to allow Mr. Tapuskovic 15 minutes. Five minutes for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There are eight questions at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will continue and you will tell me when my time has run out. I assume you will use the usual procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, in paragraphs 19 and 20 of your statement, you say that in 1986 national tensions started in the JNA. And you're mentioning the famous Keljmendi case.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did that Keljmendi do? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He killed JNA soldiers while they were asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that this is when the first tensions began between the republican Territorial Defences and the JNA, as well as the republican police forces and the JNA. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was head of the reconnaissance and notification service of Cacak municipality, and information was available to me that was not available to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as you say, it then became clear that the Territorial Defences are becoming separate armies.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Simovic told me this in his interview in 1984, and he said quite correctly, "If war breaks out one day, it will not be because Yugoslavia has been attacked by a foreign aggressor. It will be an ethnic and religious war between the Territorial Defence and the JNA." Unfortunately, that interview was also banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't go into who banned that interview. Do you consider that these tensions had at their root the nationalism and separatism of certain political structures at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Should I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have time for that. So such activities were an introduction into what was to take place later on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And to a large extent, this was in accordance with what you wrote in your book which was never published.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I mean that big work of yours where you wrote about Yugoslavia disintegrating, Greater Albania, the expulsions of Serbs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you received this information, as you say, from people close to the then-American President Reagan, that in 1992, in a meeting between Reagan and the Pope, there was talk of Yugoslavia being broken up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now -- we're now moving a long way from the witness's evidence, between any meetings of the Pope and President Reagan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in fact, the formal excuse for your dismissal from the ministry was that you had connections with the foreign intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Marko Negovanovic told me this, but they also told me that you defended me vehemently and that you pensioned off 40 generals for my sake because you wanted them to prove what they were saying and they didn't have a single piece of evidence to put before you. And now it's up to you to say whether that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was unable to dismiss generals, but whenever somebody put claims before me without evidence to support them, of course it was logical for me to ask for evidence to support certain arguments.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an occasion for me to say thank you for being on my side at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 40, you say that I asked Simovic whether he wanted the post of minister of defence and whether he wanted to work on the reorganisation of the JNA, and so on and so forth. Was it Simovic who told you this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Simovic told me this in one of our conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I won't into this, because we would simply be putting one claim against another. I don't think he could have told you this, but that's up to him. Very well, Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, as you say here that I told him that he was to work on the project of a Serbian army and so on, that for 11 years continuously I was the president, first of all of Serbia and then of Yugoslavia. Is this correct? And during those 11 years, did I establish a Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of reorganisations of the JNA, as far as I was able to follow this, because after that I was concerned mainly with preserving my own life and not what you were doing. I interrupted my work on the 1st of June, 1992, when I lost my job definitely and instituted legal proceedings, which are still going on, which are still pending to this day, and it was never established whether I was to blame for anything or whether I should get my job back. After that, I was never able to get a job in any government organ or to get a job anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I won't go into this, because I really don't know anything about this. But in your statement, in paragraph 41, it says -- or rather, you mention some sort of a viso orders. You say that I was issuing orders of this kind. I have to tell you that this is the first time I've heard of such orders, and you say that a person under certain conditions who refused to carry out such an order could be eliminated. Did you write this, or was this a mistake?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a mistake. A viso orders are ordinarily used in government organs when certain measures of readiness are in place or when there is an imminent threat of war or during war, and these orders are issued tete-a-tete, and issuing such an order meant it had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing this from your statement. Tell me, do you have any experience, any personal experience, of me giving such an a viso order?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received one from you personally, but others said that when they came to see you and when you told them something, they were not allowed to respond with a single word. They simply had to carry out the order. When I asked General Simovic, "How can you mobilise someone when you don't have legal authority to mobilise anyone?" he said, "He's my president, and I cannot say I won't do it or I can't do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that I ordered Simovic to mobilise someone?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what he dictated to me, he said that a certain number of volunteers were to be mobilised in one day, to bring up to manpower level Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you have just said is contradictory, because to mobilise excludes any kind of volunteering. Volunteers and mobilised soldiers are two quite different things.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you know that's not how things were. People are often mobilised and then in their military booklets it was recorded that they had volunteered. There were many such examples. And I came across these. Many came to complain about this at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean if someone complained that they had been registered in error as a volunteer, did you then relieve them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "relieve them"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you then have to send them to the organs mobilising soldiers? You couldn't tolerate forged books or false books.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know the case of the taxi drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What taxi drivers? I don't know anything about this incident.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the army was mobilising their conscripts and sending them off to the war-affected areas, people got scared. They left behind their equipment, trucks, everything they had taken with them, they left it in the war-affected areas and fled, and this equipment and these APCs had to be brought back to Belgrade, so we recruited taxi drivers to organise themselves as volunteers and bring back this equipment, these vehicles. Later on, it transpired that nobody wanted to receive these taxi drivers, that nobody wanted to inscribe into their military booklets that they had been at the war front, that they had been mobilised. We even asked you to intervene. And then -- and then in the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they went and brought back this equipment?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. But they didn't get anything for it. It wasn't even put into their military booklets that they had done this. Mr. Uskokovic did this, the president of the taxi drivers' association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who Mr. Uskokovic is.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And do you know what happened later? Colonel Velimirov, who was in charge of all this, ascribed to himself, or somebody gave him, the rank of general as a reward because the soldiers had heroically carried out their obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I won't ask you about this. I'm really not interested. Look at paragraph 48 of your statement. You say, as far as I can understand, that on the 20th of September, 1991 you were, as you say, angry - and I assume you were also sincere - and you said the following to Simovic. I'm quoting you: "General, Yugoslavia no longer exists. This nation expects you to save their soldiers, their children, to create a Serbian army, to be their commander." Were these your words?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I argued with him then. I argued a lot. Because I had been brought back, through the court, to my post of chief of the reconnaissance and notification service, and they wouldn't give me the documents I had created, they wouldn't let me work, nobody wanted to protect me, and I said to General Simovic that I would sue him because he wasn't intervening in my case. Nobody proved --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your case. But you said, "The people expect you to save their children, to be the war commander, to command the soldiers."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "children," I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point is here to create a Serbian army. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, we had talked about a Serbian army, when I was in the cabinet with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this your idea that he should create a Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't my idea. But before that, in the days preceding this - and it's in the paragraphs that you skipped over - it says that he talked to you about setting -- about creating a draft bill on the armed forces of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, drafting a bill is one thing and forming a Serbian army is quite another. A Serbian army was never established.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was said that the volunteers were the backbone of the future Serbian army, which would be above party interests and would defend the interests of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were a number of volunteer detachments which had nothing to do with either the state or any kind of conception. In paragraph 50, you say that Simovic spoke before the Serbian parliament when he took his oath as minister.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that this speech was a page and a half long and that it fascinated all of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say. Do you have a copy of this speech?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had a cassette, but the OTP would not accept it and we sent it back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that he read a speech that you wrote for him. I didn't suggest it to him.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. We wrote the speech together. I wrote it; he added things, corrected things. And then he brought the speech to you, and you agreed that he could read that speech out before the parliament. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what he told you. And you wrote the speech.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wrote it together. I was typing it and drafting it, and he was adding parts of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't burden you with this any longer. But judging by everything, even by your statement, the setting up of a Serbian army, which is both implicitly and explicitly ascribed to me, does not hold water. In paragraph 68, you say that a meeting was held between me and Simovic. And you say that I then told Simovic to prepare lists of JNA generals to be pensioned off. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Simovic dictated this to me after coming back from your office. That's what he told me, that he'd come back from seeing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what we concluded together here, during this examination, is it clear or should it be clear that neither I, as president of Serbia, nor Simovic, as the minister of defence of Serbia, were able to dismiss or replace or pension off JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said to General Simovic, "What did you say to President Milosevic about this?" And he said, "I said I understand." I said, "How could you say that when you're not competent to do this?" And he replied, "But he's my president."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How could Simovic have pensioned off any JNA general? How could anyone give someone a task for which he is not competent?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't competent and he didn't pension anyone off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Isn't there a clear criterion for people to be pensioned off; their age, their years of service, their rank?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this, Comrade President, but he kept telling me that you were asking him to pension off the incompetent generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, I really cannot go into what somebody told you, but do you have any knowledge of the fact that the vast majority of generals or colonels or captains or whatever rank were pensioned off, that they were pensioned off exclusively according to the criteria for retirement, which has to do with years of service and their age and also their rank? The higher the rank, the higher the age. But this is all within a range of a few years, not more. And that this is how they retired.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comrade President, I'm not saying that this is not correct, but I still abide by the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. Let's move on. Then you go on to say that I told Simovic to form lists of volunteers and to establish a battalion of volunteers. That was what you say.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He told you that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have a notebook in which I wrote this down with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But don't you know that the volunteers came under the competence of either the JNA or the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Comrade President, you must know that those volunteers went to report to the centre for reconnaissance and notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was according to the decrees that we looked through. We can't go back to that. Everybody reports to the territorial body that then registers them, has them written down in their lists, and then it is the commanders of the military units of the ranks of brigade and higher ones to okay this. That's what it says in the rules.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it looked like. They would report to the notification centres, and they would give their particulars. Then through the notification centres all the data and information would go to the republican centre for notification, and then the republican centre for notification would go down the horizontal chain and vertical chain and inform others. And the centre for notification would every day receive reports from the notification centres as to how many volunteers had signed up in which place, in which locality. Then those volunteers were further sent on to the training centres, which came under the authority of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, everything that you say is what is contained in the instructions and provisions that we looked through a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was all done -- this procedure was all in conformity with those provisions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 69, you go on to talk about the owner of Jugoskandik, who came to the ministry and said that he would help. Who sent him in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I invited him to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, you invited him to come. Now, as far as I understood it, I asked you who that man was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later, when he wanted to have a meeting with you. You said, "Who is the man?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he asked for something through you. He asked me to receive him through you, and I asked who the man was.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through General Simovic. You asked General Simovic who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then you go on to say that in October I told Simovic to ask Babic - and Babic, I assume, was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Montenegro or what? What is he, defence minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
