utterances.text: Defence minister in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So he asked his colleague why Dubrovnik was under siege?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what General Simovic asked Babic, yes. Our President Milosevic would like to know why they are moving towards a siege of Dubrovnik, for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did Babic answer? I wasn't able to establish that.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Montenegrins didn't want to go to other battlefronts and there were a lot of soldiers who were shut up in the barracks in Croatia. And the Croats did not want to release those young soldiers who were being captured there and held in the prisons, and that Prevlaka was the problem and that Montenegro had a large number of volunteers and that they had started out in the direction of Dubrovnik to instil fear in Croatia, to prevail upon them to free those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean Babic gave the explanation that pressure was being brought to bear on Croatia, to release the soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard. That's what I noted down on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I just want to hear your explanation. That's what I wanted to hear, and thank you for giving it. Now, in paragraph 97, you say that Simovic on the occasion told Babic that the JNA in 1991, in addition to its proper relationship, even when it was proclaimed an occupation army in Croatia, that it was doing everything to prevent internationality conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was that indeed the endeavours made by the JNA and was that General Simovic's conviction based on everything he knew, although he wasn't in the JNA structure any more but was the defence minister of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is that what he told Babic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was there a joint meeting of any kind between them and that the general assessment was made that a further transformation of the JNA could not be done without the political agreement of all the republics who wished to remain within the composition of Yugoslavia, to remain within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they discussed, and they also discussed how they could negotiate with Bosnia-Herzegovina, to have Bosnia-Herzegovina remain within Yugoslavia too. And then Colonel Kovacevic, I think he was, said, "Well, the defence minister in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a Croat. How are we going to negotiate with them?" And then Babic said, "But Montenegro quite certainly is going to remain with Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what happened; Serbia and Montenegro formed the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Macedonia was to be a part of that. And as far as I recall, you went to negotiations there to see the possibility of Macedonia remaining within that entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting of all the presidents of the republics, and I did advocate the preservation of Yugoslavia. There's no doubt there. Now, in your article published in Nin magazine, you say in paragraph 115 that "Milosevic didn't place the veto on the first article that appeared in Nin or any other articles in the series." Now, I'm asking you why would I place my veto on those articles?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the articles happened to be contrary to Serbia's policies and the policy you pursued. You had the right -- you had the discretionary right to use your power of veto to stop the article being published. You did not do that, and once again I would like to say thank you to you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any example where I banned any articles that were supposed to appear in any newspapers?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't deal with that at all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to tie this up to what we started off with, because we made a clear delineation and distinction, and I think we can say black and white, we put it in black-and-white terms, and distinguished between the paramilitaries and the volunteers. You spoke about that yesterday and we cleared up that issue today. So you devote a significant portion of your statement to volunteers. And in paragraph 146, you state -- yes, paragraph 146, you state that, "All the chaos at the battlefield was caused by armed groups which were under the control of the parties." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And let me just check paragraph 146. I have the sentence here, the one I quoted. "I know that Vuk Draskovic set up the Serb guards. Seselj organised his Chetniks, and those paramilitaries were located in the territory of Croatia populated by a Serb majority. And these volunteers --" I apologise to the interpreters for going so fast. "Those volunteers, at the outset, were outside the command of the JNA. Later on I heard that the volunteers had seized vehicles, money, and property, houses from the Croats." And then we come to this critical sentence, which I would like to emphasise: "All this chaos was created by the armed groups, which were under the control of the parties. That is my personal opinion and what I know." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For context, the next sentence ought to be read as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would read it. Just a moment, let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "It was obvious that it was not possible to set up armed units in a Communist or a post-Communist country with a strong army without the prior approval of the competent authority organs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, you now have -- just a moment. You have ten minutes more, so that you know that. That will give Mr. Tapuskovic 15 minutes, the Prosecution 10 minutes. Now, we'll go back to the statement. Yes, the witness was going to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I learnt about all these things, not only while I was the chef de cabinet but also while I was a journalist, when I had no fixed job, before I became the chef de cabinet, about the party armies that went to the territories in order to protect the Serb population there. I also learnt about this and I describe that in detail in my book. According to what Milan Paroski told us, he said that he was taking his army to those areas, regions. And I also learnt from Pejicic, who was in our cabinet - and this is again described in my book - that they, too, transported some of their army outside the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the SPO, the Vuk Draskovic resistance movement?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this intervention of Mr. Nice was a very good idea to have this read in context because it shows that armed units could not have been formed without the acquiescence and approval from the organs of authority, the ones that created this chaos in the first place. Now, can you explain to those who do not find this quite clear that, as far as I'm concerned at least, and the authorities that I would wield influence on, that is, the Serbian government and its organs, the organs of that institution, the organs of that government, armies of that kind could not gain support, Vuk Draskovic's army or Jovic's army or any of the others. And we have already noted that these armies were outside the system, that they were party armies, and that they were armies of oppositional political parties.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Giska, Beli, Lainovic, all these were said to be members of the state security. That's what they said in my cabinet. Now, I haven't proof and evidence of that, but that is what I heard in the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is quite unbelievable that the state security here, which as a whole, everything it does is being ascribed to me, that it should suddenly help armies that were working to overthrow me.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They assisted the protection of the Serb populace in the areas in which they were under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 147, you mentioned Jovic's volunteers, the White Eagles, and also you say that the government opened up training centres to place the volunteers under their control or, rather, to make this kind of organisation of volunteers impossible.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the government measures were to make these political party armies impossible and to prevent this kind of chaos. And I quote you when you said that all this chaos was created by the armed groups who were -- which were under party control. So the Serb government took measures to eliminate groups of this kind, and the volunteers who wished to defend their people, the people and the state, had to join up pursuant to the laws and regulations and come under the organisation of either the JNA or the Territorial Defence. That was the purpose of this Serbian government measure.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the time up to this provision and after the provision. Up to the provision, the government and you were in favour of legalising all the volunteers, of having them registered, and having their status being made equal to the reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But before the provision, there were party armies which went to the war-threatened territories without any consultations or any knowledge on the part of the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So that's quite clear. Without any consultations or knowledge of the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I learnt there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Fine. Now, is it clear that the government of Serbia - and we have seen the provisions and decrees and all the endeavours made - that they did all this, in fact, in order to prevent these party armies from running wild, running amok in the regions engulfed by war?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And my first agreement with the Prosecution was, yes, I worked on the basis of legal provisions and regulations which I was acquainted with as soon as I arrived at the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, you devote 14 paragraphs of your statement, from 155 to 169 - and as you've just heard, I don't have the time to go through all this - but you devote those paragraphs to Vuk Draskovic's Serbian Guards, that is to say, the main oppositional party. And you say that he was responsible for disseminating, looting, hatred, and the looting and the victims of war in Croatia, the casualties of that war.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what was talked about in the ministry while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also claim that he called up the JNA reservists not to respond to the mobilisation call and to use their weapons and equipment and move -- and to join up with the Serb Guards.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And I publish all my letters and correspondence with Vuk Draskovic, my conversation with Pejicic, and on the basis of everything it says in the book you can learn a lot, a lot more than I am able to present before this court of law. I maintain that what is in the book is meritorious and, therefore, an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Nice, as you say you learnt about the volunteers from the different irregulars -- you've learnt about the irregularities, the looting, the crimes that were being committed, and whether he informed me of that, and your answer was - and I jotted it down - you hope that Simovic conveyed that information to me. That was your answer. But you don't know whether he actually did so, whether he informed me of everything he heard from the volunteers. You said you hoped he conveyed it to me.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't hear what you were talking about tete-a-tete, so I couldn't say that I heard him tell you that. I said I hoped that he conveyed it all to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, as my time is almost up, is it true and correct that in the armed forces of Yugoslavia, that means -- this refers to the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and the Territorial Defence, that there were strict rules and regulations with respect to the application of international war law in our -- with respect to the armed forces of the SFRY and that they also related to the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence and that they insisted upon that; that is to say, that all higher military instances in Yugoslavia insisted upon having that prevail?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You expect me to say yes, but you know very well that this was not within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter what I expect. I am simply putting questions, and you can respond according to your conscience.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my conscience, Colonel Djokovic would say that when the reservists went to the battlefield, even the most respectable of them came back with a car full of goods, even the most honest of them did that. He would wait for them with his unit to stop them and to take records of all this, but they would fire shots from their cars, so he couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely this was part of the chaos that the leadership of Serbia was trying to prevent with these measures of discipline and with these attempts to introduce order into the situation with these units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so. Did they say anything to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it's the last question, I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said Simovic, how long was he minister of defence, how many months?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially two and a half. Unofficially, three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that during that time he published 200 interviews given to local journalists and about 100 more given to foreign journalists, 170.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is three interviews a day during his term of office.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have these interviews. I can give them to you if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how could he do anything else if he spent all his time giving interviews?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very expeditious there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Glisic, there are many topics that you deal with in your book, but there is only one thing I would like you to confirm or not confirm, as the case may be, and that is in the chapter entitled "Arkan's Sniper." In English, it's page 39. And in that passage, it's the paragraph before the last, "Shooting a rabbit with Arkan's sniper." There was a TV event broadcast via Studio B. And you said that Arkan, when asked, said, "We do not recognise anyone. We do everything on our own."

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is another topic I would like to go into before this Bench, and it concerns primarily the functioning of the Territorial Defence during decades, starting from 1984, and of course the establishment of armies after 1990. Please look at paragraph 129 of your statement. I have to read it to avoid misunderstanding. It isn't long. "The TO units did not leave their territory. They carried out their wartime assignments only on the territory of their village, town, municipality, or republic, while the JNA units were mobile all over the territory of the SFRY and their purpose was to protect the country from foreign aggressors. During times of peace, plans were drawn up relating to the movements of the reservists of the JNA." My question is as follows: Does this mean that the Territorial Defence was envisaged as a defence system in case the borders were attacked or, rather, if there was an attack, the borders would be protected by the army and the people would defend the entire territory?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Territorial Defence was to protect the territory on which they were based.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From a foreign aggressor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from a foreign aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you now look at paragraph 137 of your statement. "Should the country be attacked from outside, members of the TO units had their uniforms at home," and this was the same all over the territory of Yugoslavia; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. But that's how things were in Cacak where I saw this; I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that that's what the law prescribed.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The weapons were stored in TO depots at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 38. I have to draw your attention to these paragraphs because I would like to put this in a certain order for the Court to understand better. I'm not trying to confuse you. In paragraph 38, you say that you met General Simovic for the first time in 1984, when he was the commander of the Territorial Defence of Serbia, and that he then told you that if there was a war, this would be a war between the JNA and the TO, which was being established along ethnic lines. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he then explain something to you about the reorganisation of the JNA and the TO when the constitution was enacted and that this was based on the regulations of 1974, when the constitution was promulgated?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to explain this to you in a broader context?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Sorry, there's no time. But is this based on the constitution of 1974?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me explain to you who were the members of the TO and who were the members of the reserve forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, believe me, there's no time. Let me move on, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would the Judge give us time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if His Honour will allow, I do not object.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness is asking for time to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are very short, I'm afraid, because we've got to leave this courtroom to allow another case to come in. So I think if we'd keep it short, please. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 20. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say that as early as 1986 -- you say Simovic in 1984 and already in 1986 you're say that the territorial defences of the republics were growing stronger and becoming separate and independent armies more and more. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 189.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we haven't burdened you with this statement, of course. It's a very long statement and 50-odd pages would be available should you want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. We can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look -- now, what did I say? What paragraph? Sorry. 179, where you say that in 1991, when it seemed that conflicts could not be avoided, Slovenia and Croatia created their own republican armies out of the TO. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for having to take you back to paragraph 139 now. You say here in your last sentence, "In Croatia in 1991, most of the materiel was confiscated by the Croats and that's why the Serbs in Croatia were left without weapons." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, paragraph 269: "The Croatian TO became a parallel army, parallel with the JNA. The JNA was soon isolated and its communications were cut off. The Serbian populace could not efficaciously oppose the ZNG." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then soldiers were imprisoned in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence of Serbia ever gain the status of an army? Did it at any moment have the status?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now paragraph 49, if there's time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 40. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the creation of a Serbian army here and in the last sentence. I won't take you back to what you've already said, but in paragraph 121, you said, in the middle here, "This did not succeed because at that time Slobodan Milosevic could not confront the leadership of the JNA directly." Is this in fact what you said in your book, that the minister of defence had no authority over the JNA and also that the president of the republic had no authority over the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what mistake did I make here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just asking for your response. And to round off this topic, I did have a few other questions, but I've come to the end now. You started working in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia only in October.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of September, 1991 I received my -- the decision, the official document on the 1st of October. But I was physically present there from the 25th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And up to then you were in Cacak?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- and lived in Cacak up to the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first refugees that turned up came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much earlier, before I arrived in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I know. But these were the first refugees that started moving on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question is: Did you ever hear of the existence of any plan, at that time, planning the persecution of anyone? For example, that plans were drawn up in your ministry to persecute non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary; I worked in the same office with a Croat in the 13th of May. Not a single Croat was persecuted or dismissed from his job. No one was persecuted. They all kept their jobs, even those who came from the territories of other republics got jobs in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I contradict myself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's up to Their Honours to judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've only got one question, I think, on the book. But at some stage the Chamber may want to decide what it should do about the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll probably have to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That would be our submission. It's a book as to the accuracy of which the witness has attested and the accused seems to have accepted that it's her accurate recollection, even if he challenges some of her underlying conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On page 41 in the English - and that will match page 60 in the original - there was a line that the accused put to the witness coming from Arkan saying, "We do not acknowledge any authority. We do everything on our own." And it may be that the Chamber would want to see the context for that. Because, Ms. Gajic-Glisic, isn't this the case that as your book reveals, Arkan's arrival -- I beg your pardon, "Arkan being spoken to by the moderator --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let counsel finish, and then you can object. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- asked Arkan in public who was his commander-in-chief." Silence in the office as you were watching the broadcast, expecting him to say Simovic. He said, "Patriarch Pavle." "Everybody laughed. It was not serious. It was just his way." You then go on, then saying: "We do not acknowledge any authority. We do everything on our own." And follow that by saying, "A few days later Kum brought us a videotape shot by Studio B showing the volunteers sending their greetings to General Simovic, proclaiming him to be their commander-in-chief. Some of the officials resented that. Simovic was not one of them." You told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to correct a minor point, his not acknowledging anyone. This was not a question put by me but by Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is page 41 was put by you, but I may be wrong. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it was put by Mr. Tapuskovic, I accept that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please tell us this, please, Ms. Gajic-Glisic: You gave an account of who Arkan answered to right at the beginning. Namely, to who?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom Arkan answered at the beginning? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You told us at the beginning of your evidence who he answered to, which body he answered to.

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Comrade Zoran Sokolovic told us, they answered to the SUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that broadcast, given that he had his funny ways, was there anything to throw doubt on your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we expected him to say, "Our commander-in-chief is General Simovic," because General Simovic had declared that the volunteers were the backbone of the future Serbian army, which would transcend political parties and would defend Serb national interests, and the Serb Volunteer Guard was part of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke of a viso orders. You described how the accused made such orders, you spoke of them being appropriate at the time of an imminent threat of war. Was what the accused was doing consistent with what a man in his position should be doing with an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a viso orders was something that was quite usual in the organs of state administration, and I said sometimes I gave a viso orders to my collaborators and this was quite usual for a viso orders to be given directly tete-a-tete for a superior to give his subordinate such an order. Of course, I was not present when Mr. Milosevic spoke to people. I was not present, I did not hear him directly give a viso orders to anyone. I just heard General Simovic say, "President Milosevic told me this, this, and this," and I would note it down. I have my diaries here which I can show you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short because of time. You did in your answer make a linkage of this type of order to the imminent threat of war. The question was whether what the accused was doing, on the basis of what Simovic told you, was consistent with there being such an imminent threat or his acting as if there was such an imminent threat. Can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that in some borderline municipalities an imminent threat of war was proclaimed. So one could say that he respected those regulations in that case. But as for a viso orders, you have had so many military people here who could tell you about this off the top of their heads. They could talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on. You were asked about shelling from one country to another. Shelling from one country or one part of Yugoslavia to another. Do you know of your own knowledge where Vukovar and East Slavonia was shelled from? Was it always from within or was it ever from without its own borders?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a question raised by the accused as to whether Badza was or was not a volunteer. And he asked you a question about it linked with another question that drew a single answer. It's on page 38, line 15. Just for clarification, was Badza a volunteer or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Comrade Zoran Sokolovic told us, he had been sent from the Ministry of Defence to help Arkan and to help the populace in those areas. Whether he volunteered to go, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked questions by the accused about actions of the air force in Vukovar at the time when Arkan emerged from Vukovar. It was suggested by him, the accused, that there were a lot of civilians present. Was the air force put into action on account of civilians or on account of Arkan's predicament?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vukovar, there were quite a few civilians, both Serb and Croat civilians, of course, but the action there then was precisely because of the situation Arkan found himself in. That's why General Simovic asked the air force simply to fly over but not to fire any shots. And President Milosevic asked General Simovic to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My next question relates to that. I think the word "entreating" was used, the accused claiming that he was entreating Simovic, and Simovic then did what he did. Did you ever hear of or see Simovic denying the accused anything he asked of him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In their relationship, that is the accused and Simovic, did Simovic ever deny the accused something that the accused asked of Simovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did the accused deny? Did President Milosevic deny that Simovic denied? Who denied?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Did -- when the accused asked Simovic to do something, did Simovic always do it or did he ever refuse to do it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were things he couldn't do. He didn't make lists of incompetent generals, he didn't mobilise anyone, but he didn't tell the president he wouldn't do it. Most often he did what President Milosevic told him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two last questions. The question of paramilitaries being illegal, were you ever aware of any paramilitaries being pursued on the grounds that they were unlawful?

utterances.speaker: DOBRILA GAJIC-GLISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some proceedings were initiated before courts, and I know that Vojislav Kostunica with his team put himself at the disposal of the accused as their Defence counsel. However, most often when we received information that war crimes had been committed by these illegal paramilitary formations, we didn't know when or where or who or their name, so we were unable to investigate to a large extent. And time was short. All this happened within the space of two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The volunteers supported by or through the Ministry of Defence, once they'd been trained, where did they go and serve? They were deployed in units of the Territorial Defence of the place -- or rather, of places that were at risk, where there was a threat of genocide over the Serbian population, and they had the same treatment as the population of that place, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as you say in your summary, that's in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: C-062. Very well. Mrs. Gajic-Glisic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could the legal officer come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 23rd day of October, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
